extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of dramatic composition (tragic dramatists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama: how to construct a single unified plot, handle recognition and reversal, portray character, arrange episodes, and produce tragic effect (pity and fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single unified plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A well constructed plot should be single in its issue, rather than double.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot ought to be of one action that leads to a single reversal/unravelling; practice of the stage shows tragedies based on the fortunes of a few houses (e.g., Oedipus, Orestes). Avoid multiplicity of plots—tragedy is spoiled by an epic-like multiplicity. Example praise: plays that keep to one issue are the most tragic in effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of fortune: good to bad from error (hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune should be not from bad to good, but, reversely, from good to bad; it should come about as the result not of vice, but of some great error or frailty in a character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disastrous change should derive from a mistake/frailty (hamartia), not mere vice. This produces pity and fear; many classical examples (Oedipus) follow this principle. Those who object to tragic endings miss that 'the right ending' (an unhappy ending) produces the true tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-thread/episodic plots (Odyssean structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots with a double thread (as in the Odyssey), producing opposite catastrophes for good and bad, are secondary and appeal to popular weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such multiplicity yields pleasure of a different kind (not true tragic pleasure) and tends toward epic or comic structures; prefer unity and a coherent single action for tragic dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke pity and fear by plot structure (not spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means; but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is the better way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot ought to be so constructed that, even without the aid of the eye, he who hears the tale told will thrill with horror and melt to pity. Producing effect by spectacle or the monstrous is less artistic and dependent on extraneous aids; tragedy's proper pleasure comes from imitation (mimesis) affording pity and fear through incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select incidents among those who are near (kinship/friendship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of producing pity or terror must happen between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent—but strongest when near or dear to one another (kinship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If, for example, a brother kills a brother, or a son his father, these situations arouse the strongest pity. The poet may not destroy traditional framework but ought to show invention and skilfully handle traditional material. Such family histories supply moving incidents necessary for tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer deed done in ignorance with discovery afterwards
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three possible modes for a terrible deed: done consciously with knowledge, done in ignorance with kinship discovered afterwards, or the agent is about to do it and discovers before acting. The best is the deed perpetrated in ignorance with discovery later; the worst is being about to act knowing and then not acting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The discovery after the deed yields startling effect without gratuitous shock. 'About to act and then not act' is shocking without being tragic (no disaster follows) and is therefore rarely found in poetry. Examples: Oedipus (deed outside drama, discovery after), Medea (witting murder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of Character there are four things to be aimed at. First, and most important, it must be good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any speech or action that manifests moral purpose will be expressive of character; the character will be good if the purpose is good. This rule is relative to each class: even women or slaves may be 'good' in their class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: propriety (appropriate traits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second, the poet must aim at propriety—traits should be appropriate to the person's class/sex/status (e.g., manly valour suits a man, not a woman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attributing generally inappropriate dominant traits to a class (e.g., a consistently 'manly' character as a general female type). Propriety is judged relative to the class portrayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: likeness to life / probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirdly, character must be true to life: this is distinct from goodness and propriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A character's speech and action should conform to what is probable or necessary in life; the poet should aim at portraying types that are recognizable and believable even when ennobled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth point: consistency—for though the subject of imitation who suggested the type be inconsistent, still he must be consistently inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when portraying a person with contradictory traits, represent them in a way that is internally coherent over the course of the play. Examples of faults: Menelaus in Orestes (gratuitously bad), Iphigenia at Aulis (inconsistent character across plays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions and character must follow necessity or probability
rubrics_metrics.description: As in plot structure, in portrayal of character the poet should always aim either at the necessary or the probable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events in complication and unravelling must arise from the plot itself by necessary or probable sequence; do not rely on irrational or unexplained turns within the action. If irrational elements are unavoidable, place them outside the scope of the tragedy (e.g., as reported or foretold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Deus ex Machina within the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deus ex Machina should be employed only for events external to the drama—for antecedent or subsequent events which lie beyond the range of human knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use gods or contrived devices to resolve the central action or to produce key reversals inside the drama; this undermines the unity and probability of the plot (examples cited: Medea, Return of Greeks in the Iliad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ennoble the imitation (idealisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Tragedy is an imitation of persons who are above the common level, the poet should, while reproducing the distinctive form of the original, make a likeness which is true to life and yet more beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the example of good portrait-painters: preserve the type but 'ennoble' it so characters are vivid and elevated (Achilles as portrayed by Agathon/Homer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory appeals are concomitants but not essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not neglect appeals to the senses, which, though not among the essentials, are the concomitants of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is room for error in sensory appeal (spectacle, stagecraft), but these should support—not replace—the structural qualities that produce tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis): avoid token-based recognitions as least artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition by signs (tokens, bodily marks) is the least artistic form; formal proofs or tokens for the express purpose of proof are less artistic modes of recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congenital signs (e.g., special spears) or acquired tokens (scars, necklaces, ark) can be used but admit of more or less skilful treatment; they are inferior to recognitions emerging naturally from incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by incidental turn (better)
rubrics_metrics.description: A better kind of recognition is that which comes about by a turn of incident (e.g., the Bath Scene in the Odyssey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognitions arising through plot turns feel more natural and artful than token-based proofs; they integrate recognition into the event sequence of the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recognitions invented by the poet (speech-revelation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions invented at will by the poet (e.g., a character plainly declaring identity when the plot does not require it) are wanting in art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let recognitions emerge from what the plot necessitates, not from convenient speeches that the poet inserts merely to inform the audience or resolve a knot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by memory (sensory-triggered recollection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition may depend on memory when the sight or sound of some object awakens a feeling (e.g., Odysseus weeping at a song, hero seeing a picture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form—emotion awakened by sensory stimulus—is a natural and acceptable means of recognition when skilfully treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by process of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition may occur by a process of reasoning (deduction from resemblance, circumstance, or natural inference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical inference by characters (e.g., 'no one resembles me but X; therefore X has come') can furnish convincing recognition when it arises naturally from the situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest form: recognition arising from the incidents themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all recognitions, the best is that which arises from the incidents themselves, where the startling discovery is made by natural means (e.g., Oedipus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such recognitions dispense with artificial tokens; they are most artistic and convincing because they are integral to the plot's causal fabric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize the scene and stagecraft to avoid inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing the plot and working it out with the proper diction, the poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vivid visualization helps the poet detect inconsistencies (stage business, entrances/exits). Also work out appropriate gestures: those who feel emotion should display convincing physical signs. Failure to visualize leads to stage errors that offend audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct story: outline first, then episodes, then detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the poet takes the story ready-made or constructs it, he should first sketch its general outline, and then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure episodes are relevant to the main action; in drama episodes should be short and directly related (epic has room for extended episodes). Example: Iphigenia—outline the main turn, then place relevant episodes that support the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep episodes relevant and proportionate (drama vs epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes are the extension of the epic element; in drama they should be short and relevant so as not to produce an epic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making a tragedy have an epic structure (multiplicity and length of episodes). Poets who dramatise entire sagas (e.g., whole Iliad) usually fail on stage; select portions that serve the tragic unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: Complication and Unravelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts—Complication and Unravelling (Dénouement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complication = what comes between the beginning and the turning-point to good or bad fortune; Unravelling = from the beginning of the change to the end. The identity of a play is judged by sameness of both parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of tragedy and aim to combine merits
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of Tragedy—Simple, Complex (depending on Reversal and Recognition), Pathetic (motive is passion), Ethical (motives ethical); supernatural kinds are excluded here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should endeavour to combine all poetic merits, or at least the greatest number and the most important. Critics expect excellence across lines; choose the most important merits if not all can be achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of action: craft reversals to produce probable effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversals should be skilful and aim to produce a tragic effect that satisfies moral sense—e.g., the clever rogue outwitted, the brave villain defeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversals must remain probable in the poet's sense and not merely surprising; skill in arranging reversals helps to hit popular taste and achieve the proper tragic emotion.
